When to bring in a developer: One guide lists stalled debugging loops, sensitive data without a security review, and a production build the AI tool hasn't finished as the main triggers. Hiring too early wastes money; hiring too late costs a lot more in lost time and rework. A developer blog suggests staying on Lovable if you have under 200 users and no revenue. For 200–500 users with occasional bugs, it proposes a roughly one-week contractor engagement (around $3K). For 500+ users with recurring bugs, it suggests a full rescue or rebuild. Cost: One agency-published guide puts freelance Lovable developers at $50-150/hour or $5,000-$15,000 per project; agencies run $13,000-$25,000 for a full production build.
Where to look: Freelance platforms can be filtered for React, TypeScript, and Supabase experience, since that's the stack Lovable generates. The Lovable Discord community is another option, though it is peer-to-peer rather than an official channel. Freelancers on Fiverr advertise services covering broken authentication, Supabase issues, and Stripe integrations.
Before you hire: Prepare a written description of what needs fixing, make sure a developer can access your GitHub repo, and decide whether you need a one-time fix or ongoing support.
Caveat: The RapidDev guide is published by an agency that sells these services, so its pricing may skew high.

The search turned up a range of vibe-coded app security audit options, from vendor services to DIY checklists. Most of the statistics come from vendor marketing, so treat them as unverified.

**Commercial audit services**

A post-launch live-site scan is $19, and continuous protection is $39 per month.
- **VibeAudit** describes itself as a security and code-quality audit service for apps built with tools like Lovable, Bolt, or Cursor. Its Trustpilot page has a 0.0 score with no reviews shown, so there is no independent customer feedback to go on.
- **Softwarium** offers a vibe coding security audit and cites a figure that 65% of vibe-coded production apps contain security issues. It doesn't name the underlying study, so I'd check that figure before relying on it.

**Guidance and frameworks**
- **Cleveroad** published a checklist article. It recommends starting with exposed secrets, broken authorization, and unsafe database queries. It also argues that a checklist alone isn't enough and that the running product must be tested to confirm fixes work.
- **instinctools** describes a "vibe coding audit" as an emerging service category. It covers items beyond typical code review, such as architectural drift, GDPR/HIPAA compliance gaps, and tests that look like coverage but don't validate behavior.
- **vibe-security-skill** is a free, MIT-licensed GitHub agent skill that audits vibe-coded apps for common vulnerabilities. It's a self-serve option, not a firm.

**Research context**
A 2025 Carnegie Mellon-led benchmark, as reported by Cleveroad, found that 61% of AI-generated solutions passed functional tests but only 10.5% were secure. That is a useful reason to test security separately from functionality.
